questions.knowledge_point: Simplifying Expressions by Factoring an Alternate Form of the Pythagorean Identity
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite the numerator using $1-{sin}^{2}⁡x={cos}^{2}⁡x.$

$$
\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x+1}=\frac{1-{sin}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x+1}
$$

Next, we factor the numerator as a difference of squares, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1-{sin}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x+1} & =\frac{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x+1} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}{\cancel{\operatorname{sin}⁡x+1}} \\  & =\frac{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{1} \\  & =1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Simplifying Expressions by Factoring an Alternate Form of the Pythagorean Identity

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Limit of Cotangent Function
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's attempt to evaluate the limit by direct substitution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{+}}\operatorname{cot}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡0 \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡0}{\operatorname{sin}⁡0} \\  & =\frac{1}{0},\end{aligned}
$$

which is undefined.

Therefore, to find the limit, let's sketch the graph of $y=\operatorname{cot}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{2}).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14009686/assets/1b564f91cb71a17a1449e1ff723e32f450da6304d9c3ba33cd01e2ff942bc25c.png)

As $x$ approaches $\frac{\pi }{2}$ from the right, the values of $y=\operatorname{cot}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{2})$ are positive and grow without bound. Therefore

$$
{lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{+}}\operatorname{cot}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{2})=\infty .
$$

provenance.kp_title: Computing the Limit of Cotangent Function

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Slope of the Tangent Line to a Curve Given in Implicit Form at a Point
questions.problem: Find the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,\,1)$ for the curve $5{x}^{3}-2{y}^{4}=3.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the slope at a point, we use implicit differentiation to calculate the derivative of the curve, assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(5{x}^{3}-2{y}^{4}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(5{x}^{3})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{y}^{4}) & =0 \\ 15{x}^{2}-8{y}^{3}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ -8{y}^{3}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-15{x}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{15{x}^{2}}{8{y}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

The slope of the tangent at the point $(1,\,1)$ is then given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}_{(1,\,1)} \\  & ={(\frac{15{x}^{2}}{8{y}^{3}})}_{(1,\,1)} \\  & =\frac{15\cdot {1}^{2}}{8\cdot {1}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{15}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Finding the Slope of the Tangent Line to a Curve Given in Implicit Form at a Point

questions.knowledge_point: Simplifying Expressions in Radians Using the Sum and Difference Formulas
questions.worked_solution:
First, we recall the sum formula for cosine:

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)=\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v-\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v
$$

Applying the sum formula for cosine with $u=x$ and $v=\frac{7\pi }{4}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+\frac{7\pi }{4}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{4})-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{4}) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Simplifying Expressions in Radians Using the Sum and Difference Formulas

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Range of a Transformed Function
questions.problem: Find the range of the function $f(x)=-\operatorname{sec}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})+1.$
questions.worked_solution:
The range of $\operatorname{sec}⁡x$ consists of two intervals:

$$
\operatorname{sec}⁡x\in (-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty )
$$

Horizontal shifts and stretches have no effect on the range. Therefore,

$$
\operatorname{sec}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})\in (-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty ).
$$

We can split this into two inequalities:

$$
\operatorname{sec}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})\le -1,\,\operatorname{sec}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})\ge 1
$$

To find the range of $f(x),$ we consider both intervals separately.

- Multiplying the first interval by $-1$ and adding $1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & \operatorname{sec}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})\le -1 \\  & -\operatorname{sec}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})\ge 1 \\  & -\operatorname{sec}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})+1\ge 1+1 \\  & f(x)\ge 2.\end{aligned}
$$

- Multiplying the second interval by $-1$ and adding $1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & \operatorname{sec}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})\ge 1 \\  & -\operatorname{sec}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})\le -1 \\  & -\operatorname{sec}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})+1\le -1+1 \\  & f(x)\le 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Combining both inequalities, we get 

$$
f(x)\ge 2,\,f(x)\le 0.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the range is $f(x)\in (-\infty ,0]\cup [2,\infty ).$

provenance.kp_title: Finding the Range of a Transformed Function

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating an Algebraic Function With Negative Integer Exponent
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite the integral as

$$
\int 3(1-3x)^{-3}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=1-3x.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-3\,⟹\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.
$$

We now write our integral in terms of $u,$ calculate the integral as normal, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3(1-3x)^{-3} & =3\int {u}^{-3}\cdot (-\frac{1}{3})\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\cdot (-\frac{1}{3})\int {u}^{-3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\int {u}^{-3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{(-2)}{u}^{-2}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(1-3x)^{-2}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2(1-3x)^{2}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\frac{1}{2(1-3x)^{2}}+C] & =\frac{1}{2}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\frac{1}{(1-3x)^{2}}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[(1-3x)^{-2}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-2)(1-3x)^{-3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1-3x)+0 \\  & =-(1-3x)^{-3}\cdot (-3) \\  & =3(1-3x)^{-3} \\  & =\frac{3}{(1-3x)^{3}}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Integrating an Algebraic Function With Negative Integer Exponent

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Value of an Observation, Standard Deviation, or Mean Given a Z-Score
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the value of an observation $x$ which yields a given $z$-score in a data set with mean $\overset{―}{x}$ and standard deviation $\sigma ,$ we can use the following formula:

$$
x=\overset{―}{x}+z\cdot \sigma 
$$

Substituting $x=5.08,$ $\overset{―}{x}=6.2,$ and $z=-0.7$ into the formula and solving for $\sigma ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\overset{―}{x}+z\cdot \sigma  \\ 5.08 & =6.2+(-0.7)\cdot \sigma  \\ -1.12 & =-0.7\cdot \sigma  \\ \sigma  & =1.6.\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Finding the Value of an Observation, Standard Deviation, or Mean Given a Z-Score
